papers.title: AI-Assisted Computational Reproducibility on the FABRIC Testbed
authors: Komal Thareja, Paul Ruth, Berent Aldikacti, Michael Zink
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2606.25879v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Computational reproducibility remains difficult despite being central to scientific research. In this paper, we show how the international FABRIC testbed, combined with a large language model (LLM) coding agent through LoomAI, can simplify reproducing published experiments across multiple domains. We reproduced three case studies on FABRIC, covering BBR-family congestion-control evaluations, LAMMPS molecular dynamics scaling benchmarks on a CPU-only MPI cluster, and stress protein homeostasis genomics pipelines.

papers.title: HPC-MQBench: Qualification-First Benchmarking on Slurm with a Single-Broker Kafka Evaluation
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.09786v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Messaging experiments on high-performance computing clusters must coordinate services, clients, and measurement within scheduler allocations. We present HPC-MQBench, a Slurm-orchestrated benchmark that links resumable experiment control to record checks, delivery accounting, and qualification before rate ranking. Its Kafka evaluation placed producers/controller, one broker, consumers, and monitoring on four nodes. With memory-backed logs, 120 workload configurations yielded 99 qualified observations, 14 outside the producer-delivery policy, and seven with invalid evidence. papers.title: Expert Coupling in MoE Pretraining: Reducing All-to-All Overhead with Correlated Placement and Token Shuffling
authors: Radha Gulhane, Quentin Anthony, Beren Millidge
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.09372v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers replace the feed-forward block of a Transformer with E expert networks, and each token is routed to k of these experts. Under expert parallelism (EP) the experts are distributed across GPUs, and every MoE layer runs all-to-all collectives in the forward and backward passes to dispatch tokens to their experts and then combine the results. On a cluster with 8 AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs per node, these collectives can take 45% of the training step at EP32 with top-2 routing and 60% with top-6 routing. We find that early in pretraining routers have already learned to assign tokens to experts in correlated patterns, both within a layer and across layers.
